title: Blood Pressure: What the Numbers Mean

scenes.topic: Blood Pressure: What the Numbers Mean
scenes.subtitle: Clinical Foundations
learn: when a reading counts as high
scenes.narration: In this video, we're going to talk about blood pressure, and what its two numbers really mean. It is one of the most common measurements in health care, and one of the most important. [pause] By the end, you'll know what blood pressure measures, what systolic and diastolic mean, when a reading counts as high, and how to keep it healthy.

scenes.headline: Most people with high blood pressure feel perfectly well.
scenes.question: So how would you know yours is too high?
scenes.narration: Here's the surprising part. Most people with high blood pressure don't feel any symptoms at all. The World Health Organization estimates that around 46 percent of adults with high blood pressure don't even know they have it. [pause] So how would you know that yours is too high?

scenes.plain: The force of circulating blood pushing against the walls of your arteries.
scenes.narration: So what is blood pressure? It is the force of circulating blood pushing against the walls of your arteries, the vessels that carry blood away from the heart. Every time your heart pumps, it pushes blood into those arteries, and their walls stretch to take it. We measure that pressure in millimetres of mercury.

scenes.title: Every heartbeat sends a pressure wave

callouts.label: The heart
callouts.text: pushes blood out with every beat

callouts.label: Systolic pressure
callouts.text: the peak, while the heart contracts

callouts.label: Diastolic pressure
callouts.text: the floor, while the heart rests

callouts.label: Your reading
callouts.text: the pair of values, beat by beat

scenes.narration: Let's watch it happen. With every beat, the heart pushes a surge of blood into the arteries. The elastic artery wall stretches as the pressure wave passes, then springs back. The highest pressure, while the heart contracts, is the systolic pressure. The lowest pressure, while the heart rests between beats, is the diastolic pressure. [pause] A gauge on the artery would swing between those two values with every beat, and that pair is your reading.

scenes.title: Reading the two numbers
scenes.narration: In practice, we measure blood pressure with an inflatable cuff around the upper arm, and a monitor shows two numbers. The first, or top number, is the systolic pressure, here 120. The second, or bottom number, is the diastolic pressure, here 80. Both are in millimetres of mercury, so we say this reading is 120 over 80.

scenes.title: Where does a reading fall?
scenes.caption: Hypertension is diagnosed on readings from two different days.
scenes.narration: So where does a reading fall? For most adults, a low reading is 90 over 60 or lower. The ideal range sits between 90 over 60 and 120 over 80. Between 120 over 80 and 140 over 90, you're at risk of developing high blood pressure. And a reading of 140 over 90 or higher is high blood pressure, also called hypertension. [pause] It is diagnosed when the readings are that high on two different days.

scenes.title: What years of high pressure do

steps.note: Constant pressure strains and damages artery walls
In the arteries of the brain
In the small arteries of the kidneys
Pumping against high pressure wears the heart out

scenes.narration: Why does this matter so much? Over the years, high blood pressure strains and damages the walls of the arteries. In the heart's own arteries, that damage can lead to a heart attack. In the arteries of the brain, it can lead to a stroke. In the kidneys, it causes kidney damage. [pause] And because the heart has to pump harder against the pressure, it can eventually lead to heart failure.

scenes.title: Keeping blood pressure healthy
scenes.narration: The good news is that you can do a lot to keep it healthy. Eat less salt: less than 5 grams a day, which is just under a teaspoon. Eat more vegetables and fruit. Stay physically active. Avoid tobacco, and limit alcohol. And have your blood pressure checked regularly, because that's the only way to know.

scenes.title: “I feel fine, so it must be normal.”
scenes.note: Measure it. A diagnosis needs readings from two different days.
scenes.narration: Here's the most common mistake: thinking that if you feel fine, your blood pressure must be normal. In fact, most people with high blood pressure feel nothing at all. Only a measurement can tell you. [pause] So measure it, and remember that a diagnosis needs high readings on two different days.

scenes.question: A patient's blood pressure is 150 over 95 on two different days. What does that suggest?
scenes.narration: Time for a quick check. A patient's blood pressure is 150 over 95, measured on two different days. What does that suggest? Pause the video, and think it through.

scenes.question: A patient's blood pressure is 150 over 95 on two different days. What does that suggest?
scenes.answer: High blood pressure: both numbers are at or above 140 over 90, on two different days.
scenes.narration: It suggests high blood pressure, or hypertension. The systolic value of 150 is above 140. The diastolic value of 95 is above 90. And because it was confirmed on two different days, it meets the definition.

scenes.takeaway: Know your numbers. Measure, don't guess.
scenes.narration: Let's recap. Blood pressure is written as two numbers, systolic over diastolic. A reading of 140 over 90 or higher, on two different days, is high blood pressure. And because it is usually silent, the only way to know is to measure it. [pause] Know your numbers.
